prompt: What does a step-back prompt ask for before the specific question?

choices.text: The general principle the question is an instance of
choices.why: Right. The answer to that goes into the prompt for the specific question.

choices.text: A longer, more detailed version of the same question with the tricky part underlined
choices.why: That is the instinct the technique goes against.

choices.text: A guess at the answer, to be checked later
choices.why: Nothing is answered in the first call; it asks for rules.

choices.text: A list of similar questions
choices.why: It asks for the rule behind this one, not for neighbours.

prompt: In the illustration, the direct prompt got "Yes, open until 18:00" although every fact was in the prompt. Why?
hint: Which words of the question and the handbook match most strongly?

choices.text: The handbook page was too long for the model to read
choices.why: It is four lines. Length was not the problem.

choices.text: Holiday hours were missing from the handbook
choices.why: They were there: "On public holidays the café follows the Sunday hours."

choices.text: The model cannot do arithmetic with times
choices.why: The arithmetic was fine for the rule it picked. It picked the wrong rule.

choices.text: `Wednesday` matched the weekday line first
choices.why: Right. The deciding rule was reached through *holiday*, which sat in the middle of the question.

prompt: What did the step-back reply add that the handbook did not already contain?
hint: Compare the rules list with the four handbook lines.

choices.text: The café's holiday opening hours, which the handbook left out
choices.why: The handbook had them. The step back moved them forward.

choices.text: A correction to the handbook's closing time
choices.why: Nothing was corrected; the rules repeat the handbook.

choices.text: No new fact; the same rules, laid out as rules
choices.why: Yes. The gain is in the arrangement: the holiday rule stated as a rule, and the arithmetic done once.

choices.text: The final answer to the customer's question
choices.why: The first call was told not to answer any particular question.

prompt: Put the step-back procedure in order.
hint: Two calls; the second needs the first.
items: Ask for the general rule behind the question
Get the model's statement of the rule
Put that statement into a second prompt beside the question
Get the answer to the specific question

prompt: With the ideal gas law in the prompt, the gas question became `2 / 8`. What fraction of the old pressure is the new one, as a decimal?
Who can write the step-back question?

choices.text: You, or the model itself if first asked for the more general question
choices.why: Right. Either works; the shape of the two calls stays the same.

choices.text: Only the model, since a person cannot know the principle in advance
choices.why: You often do know it, and writing it yourself is the simplest version.

choices.text: Only a person, since a model would just repeat the question
choices.why: Asked for "the more general question behind this one", a model generalises well enough to be useful.

choices.text: Nobody: the second call works it out on its own
choices.why: The step back is a separate call or instruction. It does not happen by itself.

prompt: Which question gains least from a step back?
hint: Is there a principle behind it to step back to?

choices.text: Can the kitchen take a hot food order at 11:45 on a Wednesday that is a public holiday?
choices.why: That is the lesson's example of a rule hidden by the wording.

choices.text: A refund of R$ 140 by card: can it be paid in cash, and who approves it?
choices.why: Two rules apply, one of them an exception; stepping back to the refund rules helps.

choices.text: What happens to a gas's pressure if its temperature doubles and volume grows eightfold?
choices.why: Naming the law is most of the work there.

choices.text: What is the guest Wi-Fi network called?
choices.why: Right. It is one line of the handbook, with no rule behind it.

prompt: The step-back reply states a plausible rule that is not in the handbook, and the final answer follows from it correctly. What happened, and what should you check?
hint: Where in the two calls did the error enter?

choices.text: Nothing went wrong, because the final answer follows logically
choices.why: Following logically from a false premise does not make it true.

choices.text: The second call made the error, so the fix is a better second prompt
choices.why: The second call did its job faithfully. The rule it was given was wrong.

choices.text: Lesson 5's failure, one step earlier: check the step-back reply
choices.why: Right. A final answer that follows logically from a wrong rule looks sound; the rule is the part to check against the handbook.

choices.text: Step-back prompting cannot be used with a handbook
choices.why: It worked with the handbook in the lesson. Here the rule was not in it, or not used.

prompt: The step-back version sent `step1.txt` (122 tokens) and then `step2.txt` (226). How many input tokens is that in total?
Besides the extra input tokens, what else does the two-call version cost?
hint: What does the second call wait for?

choices.text: Nothing: the second call is free because it repeats the handbook
choices.why: Every token in every call is counted, repeated or not.

choices.text: A second round trip, waiting for the first reply
choices.why: Yes. The first call's reply is output you pay for, and the second call cannot start until it arrives.

choices.text: A larger model, since step-back prompting only works on one
choices.why: No model requirement was stated; the technique is a prompt pattern.

choices.text: A fine-tuning run to teach the model the rules first
choices.why: No training is involved. The rules go in the prompt.

prompt: How can you keep most of the step-back effect in a single call?
hint: What matters is the order in which things are written.

choices.text: Ask for the general rules first and the answer after, in one prompt
choices.why: Right. The rules are still written before the answer, and you see both in one reply.

choices.text: Ask for the answer first and the rules afterwards, so that the reply comes back faster and the rules can then be checked
choices.why: Rules written after the answer cannot shape it; they can only justify it.

choices.text: Put the word "step back" in the system prompt
choices.why: The words do nothing on their own. What helps is the rules being written before the answer.

choices.text: Lower the temperature
choices.why: Temperature changes the drawing, not what is written before the answer.

prompt: How does step-back prompting differ from chain of thought (lesson 26)?
hint: What is written down before the answer, in each?

choices.text: Step-back uses one call and chain of thought always uses two
choices.why: Either can be done in one call or several; the difference is what gets written.

choices.text: Chain of thought writes nothing before the answer, while step-back always does
choices.why: Chain of thought is exactly writing steps before the answer.

choices.text: They are the same technique under two names
choices.why: They write different things: a rule, or the steps.

choices.text: Step-back writes the rule; chain of thought, the steps
choices.why: Yes. They can be combined: step back to the rule, then reason through the case.

prompt: Which of these questions is the best candidate for a step back?
hint: Look for a rule hidden behind the wording.

choices.text: What time does the bread arrive?
choices.why: One line of the handbook; there is nothing general to step back to.

choices.text: What is the café called?
choices.why: A name, not a rule.

choices.text: How many allergens does a label list?
choices.why: A single stated fact, 14.

choices.text: A loyalty customer lost their card and wants the stamps moved: is that possible without the number?
choices.why: Right. It is an instance of the loyalty rules, with a condition that is easy to miss.

prompt: Match each file to what it is.
hint: Three prompts, one capture of what they cost.

pairs.right: the handbook and the question, in one call
the handbook and a request for the general rules
the handbook, the rules and the question

prompt: Which statements about step-back prompting are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what it adds, what it costs and what it cannot do.

choices.text: It changes the order in which facts are laid out before the answer
choices.why: Yes: the rule is stated before the case.

choices.text: It costs more input tokens and a second round trip
choices.why: Yes: 348 input tokens against 116 in the lesson's example.

choices.text: It gives the model rules that are in neither the prompt nor its training
choices.why: It cannot. Without the rule, the step back states a plausible one.

choices.text: It helps most when the wording of a question hides the deciding rule
choices.why: Yes: the holiday toastie is the case.

prompt: In step-back prompting the first call asks for the general ___ behind the question, and its reply goes into the second prompt.
hint: Rule, law, category: the section's word for all three.

prompt: A tax assistant answers "Is this purchase deductible?" correctly most of the time, and badly when the purchase falls under an exception. You can afford a second call for a few hard cases. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: Exceptions hidden by wording are where the technique pays.

choices.text: Step back for those cases: first ask which rules and exceptions govern this kind of purchase, then the question
choices.why: Right. An exception to a more obvious rule is exactly the shape step-back prompting helps with.

choices.text: Step back on every question, since it is always more accurate
choices.why: On general or one-line questions it only costs a call and a third more waiting.

choices.text: Ask the same question twice and keep the longer answer
choices.why: Length says nothing about which answer applied the exception.

choices.text: Remove the exceptions from the prompt so the model is not confused
choices.why: Then the model cannot apply them at all.
